opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference comes down to data. For large language models, the paradigm was in a sense already set up for us: humanity spent decades putting text on the internet, so when researchers wanted to scale, the data was just there. The main work became architecture, compute, and figuring out how to train efficiently at enormous scale. You could follow scaling laws fairly predictably: more data, more parameters, more compute, and capabilities emerged.

Robotics doesn't have that. There's no internet of robot actions. Nobody has been uploading billions of hours of joint torques, contact forces, and motor commands paired with what the robot saw and what it was trying to do. So in robotics, data collection is itself a core research problem, not a preprocessing step. You have to decide: do we collect through teleoperation, which is high quality but expensive and slow? Do we rely on simulation, which scales but has the sim-to-real gap? Do we learn from human videos, which are abundant but lack the action labels and the embodiment matches? Each choice shapes the whole research agenda.

The second difference is embodiment. Language is fairly universal: a token is a token. But robots come in very different bodies—arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, different grippers, different sensors. An action that makes sense for one robot may be meaningless for another. So building a foundation model means figuring out how knowledge transfers across embodiments, which has no real analogue in LLMs.

Third, the physical world closes the loop. A language model can produce a slightly wrong sentence and the cost is small. A robot acting in the real world gets immediate physical consequences, errors compound over time, and evaluation is hard—you can't just run a benchmark on a server overnight; you have to run the robot, reset the scene, and measure. That makes iteration much slower and pushes you toward a different methodology: tighter coupling between hardware, data, and models, and a lot more emphasis on generalization and robustness rather than just benchmark scores.

So what we've done is borrow a lot from LLMs—the transformer architectures, pretraining on large diverse data, using vision-language models as a backbone for semantic understanding—but the paradigm itself is different. In language, you scale on existing data. In robotics, you have to build the flywheel that creates the data in the first place, and that changes almost everything about how the research proceeds.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the biggest difference comes down to data. When people built large language models, the data was already there. Humanity had spent decades writing on the internet, and you could scrape trillions of tokens essentially for free. The research question was mostly about scaling and architecture. In robotics, there is no internet of robot actions. Nobody has been recording decades of joint torques and gripper commands paired with camera images. So the central problem isn't just how to train a bigger model, it's how to get the data in the first place.

That changes the entire research loop. In language, you train once on a static corpus and evaluate on benchmarks. In robotics, data collection, model training, and real-world deployment have to form a cycle. You collect teleoperation demonstrations, you train a policy, you put it on a robot, you see where it fails, and that failure tells you what data to collect next. Simulation also plays a role that has no real analogue in LLMs. We can generate huge amounts of experience in simulation, but then we face the sim-to-real gap, which is a problem language researchers never had to think about.

The second difference is that robotics is embodied and interactive. A language model produces text and a human reads it. There's no physical consequence to a wrong token. A robot acts in the world, and its actions change the state of the world, which changes what it observes next. Small errors compound. So a robotics model needs to be good at closed-loop control, at reacting in real time, and at being safe, not just at producing a plausible output.

The third difference is about the generalization target. For language, the goal was one model that handles all text tasks. For robotics, we're also trying to generalize across embodiments. Robots have different arms, different hands, different sensors. A foundation model has to somehow abstract over all of that, which is a dimension the language community never had to deal with.

So while we borrow a lot of the architecture and the training recipes from LLMs, and vision-language models are a crucial starting point, I think of robotics foundation models as fundamentally a data-engine and embodiment problem rather than a pure scaling problem. That is why the paradigm looks different in practice, even if the models share the same lineage.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how we get data and how we learn from it. With language models, you can start with a huge amount of text that already exists. In robotics, we don’t have an equivalent internet of robot experience—observations, actions, and the consequences of those actions—at anything like that scale.

And a robot has to operate in a closed loop. It takes an action, changes the world, observes what happened, and decides what to do next. A small mistake can change everything it sees afterward. So learning to predict an action from a recorded example is useful, but it doesn’t solve the whole problem of controlling a robot.

That makes interaction central to the research paradigm. We need to think about collecting experience, learning through trial and error, using simulation, and transferring what we learn to physical hardware. The model architecture matters, but so does the entire system that generates its training experience.

So I see language models as an important starting point. They bring knowledge and reasoning capabilities. But turning those capabilities into reliable physical behavior requires more than just scaling up the same training recipe.

r002.rationale: It describes the lack of large-scale robotics experience, but does not say this is why robotics researchers generally fine-tune pre-trained models.

r003.rationale: It says robotics requires more than scaling the same training recipe and describes interaction and physical control as distinct parts of the research paradigm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is how we get data. With language models, there’s already a huge amount of text on the internet, and you can train on that data at enormous scale. In robotics, we don’t have an equivalent supply of robot experience. We have to collect it through robots interacting with the physical world, which is expensive and slow, or generate it in simulation, which introduces a gap between simulation and reality.

The data also depends on the robot: its body, its sensors, and the actions it can take. So the model, the hardware, and the data-collection process are tightly connected. You can’t treat model training as a completely separate step.

And ultimately, a robot has to act in a closed loop. Its actions change the world, and those changes determine what it sees next. So I see the paradigm as building a whole learning system—collecting experience, training, deploying, and collecting new experience—rather than simply scaling up a model on a fixed dataset.

r002.rationale: It describes the lack of an internet-scale supply of robot experience, but does not connect that limitation to generally fine-tuning already pre-trained models.

r003.rationale: The response describes robotics research as a different paradigm from language-model scaling, emphasizing hardware, data collection, and closed-loop learning rather than a one-to-one mapping.
